# Appendix: per-area assessments

**AREA-01** — raw 7, confirmed 6, refuted 0

api-execution-core is in unusually strong shape for its complexity. The run state machine (start/stop/pause/resume/adjust/scale) is consistently hardened: every durable transition has a rollback-on-persist-failure path, terminal transitions are fenced by execution-lease tokens checked transactionally, stop is fail-closed with a versioned force-upgrade retry worker, leadership epochs cancel operation contexts synchronously, retry workers exit when leadership is lost, and restart reconciliation (reconcileStoredActiveTest) prevents runs wedging in non-terminal states. Bounded-growth discipline is real (error patterns/evidence caps, per-test history byte caps, route cache LRU, group-metrics history cache LRU). The defects found are concentrated in performance/scalability -- storage I/O and multi-megabyte script serialization performed while holding the global tr.mu (the repo's known 'locks held across DB I/O' class), per-VUser-step durable persistence during ramps, and unbounded aggregate memory from boot-time history hydration -- plus two data-accuracy issues (the local goal controller's stale VUser view and usage accounting billing configured rather than actual duration). No crash, data-loss, or wedged-run defect was found.

_Boundary leads:_ pkg/api/metrics.go:52-57 builds local LiveMetrics.TotalTx/TotalErrors from per-window engine snapshots (window semantics proven at pkg/engine/metrics.go:458-475, batch cleared each publish), while the distributed path sets the same fields from FleetMetrics at pkg/api/distributed_metrics.go:431 (fleet.Count - fleet.Errors). If FleetMetrics.Count is cumulative for the run (generator side, pkg/distributed/generatorrpc/service.go), the identical WebSocket/history field 'total_transactions' silently changes meaning between local and distributed backends -- distributed-metrics/frontend areas should confirm. · pkg/api/launch_preflight.go:258 evaluateGeneratorPlacementConflictsLocked overlays tr.cachedGeneratorInventorySnapshot(); immediately after controller boot (before the first inventory refresh) the cache can be empty/stale so active targets carry zero AvailableCapacity/protocol data -- whether chooseGeneratorShardsForGroup then rejects valid launches (preflight false negative) depends on distributed assignment code outside this area (pkg/api/distributed_assignment*.go) and should be verified there.

**AREA-02** — raw 6, confirmed 6, refuted 0

This area is in unusually strong shape for its complexity. Timeslot/reservation double-booking is genuinely closed: binds, releases, approvals, and edits all go through real store transactions with reciprocal test-row updates, updated_at/revision CAS tokens, and lease-term fencing threaded through every durable write (verified down into pkg/storage/sqlite_timeslots.go — the approve/edit TOCTOU I hunted for is correctly prevented by the updated_at CAS). Occurrence idempotency (deterministic test IDs, materializing claims, transition tokens, crash-recovery reconciliation) is thorough on both the scenario and execution-plan sides, admission fails closed on reservation lookup errors, and the cron evaluator handles timezones, POSIX dom/dow OR semantics, Quartz specifiers, and leap-day horizons with tests. The defects that remain are second-order: an idempotence gap that makes conflict-blocked schedules rewrite themselves (revision++) every 30s sweep and break operators' required If-Match edits; a DST fall-back double-fire for schedules inside the repeated hour; and read-path lock/SQL amplification where the fair-share pending sort issues a reservation-store query per sort comparison under the global write lock on every test list read. Nothing found rises to data loss or corruption.

_Boundary leads:_ pkg/api/execution_plan_fencing.go:47-64 — executionLeaseTermCurrent performs a durable GetSchedulerLease SELECT on every call and is invoked once per schedule per sweep iteration while tr.mu is held (pkg/api/scheduler.go:341); under HA+Postgres that is O(schedules) lease reads inside the global lock every 30s. The lease-check design is owned by the HA/leadership area. · pkg/api/tests.go:484-741 — list/read endpoints take the global WRITE lock (refreshReadMetadataForTestList/refreshReadMetadataForTest) to refresh pending-queue metadata; that read-path locking policy belongs to the runner/tests area but is the amplifier for my fair-share ranking finding.

**AREA-03** — raw 7, confirmed 7, refuted 0

This area is in genuinely strong shape at the durability layer: the finalization/cleanup/version outboxes are token-fenced with CAS transitions, orphan recovery is identity-checked and create-only, the materialization cache has correct reader/evictor coordination (keyed gates, identity re-checks, marker-based LRU), quantiles avoid the classic percentile-remerge trap by feeding raw durations into exact-then-t-digest accumulators, and the sanitize/export path preserves counts, sizes, and hashes with change detection. The report registry (HTML/PDF/CSV from one section table) is clean and consistent. The real weaknesses cluster in two places: (1) distributed-run archives merge per-generator interval summaries by plain concatenation, which silently breaks the archived report's fleet-level headline metrics, timeline ordering, and bucket attribution for every multi-generator run; and (2) several read endpoints do full-archive work per request with no cache or streaming (manifest sanitize pre-pass, release-trend sibling-report rebuilds against a 16-entry LRU, load-comparison full-slice reads that hard-fail at 500k transactions), which turns normal-sized perf-test archives into multi-second-to-failing requests.

_Boundary leads:_ pkg/distributed/generatorrpc/service.go:1656-1690 — generators archive per-generator, per-window interval summaries (TPS/ActiveVUsers local, TotalTx per-window); fixing AREA-03's distributed report wrongness likely needs merge-time aggregation or a generator-side schema change owned by the distributed area. · pkg/api/dynatrace_dry_run.go:201 — readAllArchiveTransactions error is silently discarded, so archives over 500k records / 128MB quietly produce a dry-run with no transaction evidence (same bounded-reader hard limit as the load-comparison finding, but in the integrations area). · pkg/api/library_bundle.go:433 — sanitizedRunArchiveMetadata performs a full transactions-file sanitize pass per bundled archive during library bundle builds (same uncached full-scan seam as the manifest-endpoint finding, owned by the library area).

**AREA-04** — raw 4, confirmed 4, refuted 0

The api-import-orchestration area is in unusually strong shape for its size and churn history. The historical defect classes this repo has been burned by are now systematically defended: the shared importCommitSpec boundary (import_commit_service.go) gives OpenAPI/Postman/AsyncAPI one create/replace path with deterministic create IDs (protectedImportCreateScriptID), idempotent-replay reporting, and honest 503 partial-state responses when source retention lags the durable script write; the source-retention/commit-fence pair (import_source_retention.go, import_source_commit_fence.go) fingerprints scripts and predecessor owners so a stale retry cannot attach a source to a newer revision; the Bruno one-shot session lifecycle (claim/restore/complete with a renewing lease, publication journals, and a reference-checked janitor) is genuinely careful about crash windows; and JMeter direct-import uses receipts plus a write-ahead createImportTransaction with deterministic asset IDs and exact-equivalence adoption on retry. Preserved-update and draft-attestation logic protect user edits and credentials through masked read-modify-write. The defects that remain are second-order: a silent multi-JMX drop at the JMeter ZIP boundary, a whole-server single-slot Bruno inspect semaphore that includes the request-body network read in its critical section, and one merge-re-import edge that replaces a user-customized data source while the diff claims preservation. The main structural cost is the response-projection layer, which re-serializes the same scripts many times per import request.

_Boundary leads:_ pkg/api/script.go:846 (createScriptDurable) re-applies preparePersistentImportedLibraryScript to scripts that handleSaveJMeterImport already projected at pkg/api/handlers_import_jmeter.go:403; the crash-retry adoption path (directImportPreparedAssetsMatch, pkg/api/direct_import_idempotency.go:446) only adopts on exact equivalence, so if any projection step is ever non-idempotent a retry after a crash 500s instead of adopting the committed assets. Owned by the scripts-persistence area; worth a fixpoint test there.

**AREA-05** — raw 7, confirmed 7, refuted 0

This area is engineered to an unusually high standard: execution-epoch fencing (claim TTL derated by transit budget, per-cycle re-verification), fenced per-target metrics consumers with topology-generation revalidation at every mutation point, staged AssignWork + coordinated CommitWork barriers, and compensation/rollback on every control fanout (pause, duration, vusers, evacuation). Placement math conserves VUser totals (baseline+floor+largest-remainder with per-target caps), and metrics aggregation applies correct semantics per field (rates summed per-window, gauges maxed, process CPU averaged over active pods). The genuine weak spots are in fault tolerance for a generator that is permanently unreachable: every fail-closed path assumes the fenced party can eventually ACK an exact-generation stop, so the one scenario tolerate_generator_loss advertises (a dead generator pod) instead force-stops the whole fleet and can leave the run stuck non-terminal in STOPPING behind an unbounded retry. Secondary issues are lock-scope (a config read-lock held across cross-controller HTTP; DB reads under the global runner mutex in launch gating) and fleet-alert webhooks that only fire when someone polls the GET endpoint.

_Boundary leads:_ testexecution.go:1173 and runStopTeardownRetryWorker (testexecution.go:1273+): stopping a RUNNING distributed test whose generator is permanently unreachable appears to loop in STOPPING forever — stopTestContext (pkg/api/distributed_execution_backend.go:1370-1376) tolerates Unavailable/NotFound only when status is already COMPLETE/FAILED, and the retry worker that owns recovery lives outside this area · pkg/api/capacity.go:367 (liveInventory writer): verify tr.mu -> liveInventoryMu lock ordering holds on all paths; cachedGeneratorInventorySnapshot (pkg/api/external_runner_gating.go:569-585) acquires liveInventoryMu.RLock while callers hold tr.mu · pkg/distributed/generatorrpc/service.go:1988: the generator currently always emits FleetMetrics alongside Groups; if a batch ever carried Groups[].Metrics plus raw Transactions without FleetMetrics, aggregateDistributedMetricsBatches (pkg/api/distributed_metrics.go:74-98) would double-count group TPS from both sources

**AREA-06** — raw 6, confirmed 6, refuted 0

This area is in genuinely strong shape at its core: pkg/dslwalk is a clean, budget-enforced traversal contract that really does cover every nested surface (control.steps/else plus all four slice forms of http_sequence params.requests — I verified no other catalog action nests children); the DSL action catalog is data-driven with schemagen freshness tests (TestGeneratedSchemaIsFresh) that make catalog drift a CI failure rather than a latent bug; script CRUD in pkg/api/script.go is CAS-fenced against concurrent editors and HA replicas on every mutation path; and the masked-write reconciliation in script_projection.go, while very dense, is carefully layered with explicit fail-closed decisions and transient-gate round-trip handling. The debug manager's lease/fence/abandon-backstop lifecycle is unusually robust against wedged protocol adapters — the historical session-leak defect class appears well closed. The real defects I found are at seams rather than in the cores: the debug manager's per-event broadcasts re-serialize the entire accumulated session (quadratic cost on large imported scripts) and its logs/events retain full wire bodies uncapped; the object-repository bind-from-script flow binds nested actions by name while its ambiguity/collection scan is top-level-only (the exact mis-binding its own comment tries to prevent); one replay endpoint missed the credential-preserving-echo special case its debug sibling received; and replay progress does not count as session activity for idle-cancel purposes.

_Boundary leads:_ pkg/api/handlers_replay.go:101-112 — handleReplayScript (POST /scripts/{id}/replay) has the same missing matchesStoredScriptDisclosureProjection special case as the in-scope replay-session handler (finding 3); a shared fix should cover all three sibling endpoints · pkg/api/websocket.go:292-299 — Hub.BroadcastJSON marshals every payload even with zero subscribers, amplifying the quadratic debug-session broadcast cost (finding 1); hub is owned by another area · pkg/engine/replay.go:987 — report.Events appends one event per executed leaf including every control_loop iteration with no cap below MaxControlLoopIterations=1,000,000, so the engine-side replay report itself can grow to GBs on high-iteration debug replays; engine area owns the cap decision

**AREA-07** — raw 8, confirmed 8, refuted 0

This area is in genuinely good shape overall: optimistic concurrency is pervasive and correctly plumbed (SHA-based group-settings revisions shared by both Command Center editors, data-pool row-version CAS whose storage layer returns the incremented token, revision-fenced cursor pagination and a three-pass revision-fenced CSV export that aborts the connection rather than serving a torn file), the masked-secret protocol is reorder-safe and consistently fail-closed, the data-pool import/export round-trip (formula-guard encode/decode, engine-cap preflight, APEX-export envelope) is carefully engineered, and the typed-nil storage gotcha from past reviews now has defense-in-depth in the decoders. The engine-side row handout is shard-aware, so the classic distributed 'unique' duplicate problem does not exist. The defects found are integration seams rather than rot: the new Command Center runtime-settings editor collides with create-time iteration-override provenance, the '@'-anywhere credential heuristic over-classifies plain emails and breaks legitimate parameter/Env workflows, the schedule-health hot path counts statuses by materializing an unbounded occurrence table (polled every 5s), and the run manifest's 'initial configuration' is sourced from the continuously rewritten durable record so it mirrors current state.

_Boundary leads:_ pkg/api/persistence.go:1373 buildManagedTestRecord boxes test.Assignment/test.GoalConfig/test.RuntimeSettings directly into storage `any` fields instead of using the generatorAssignmentForStorage/runtimeSettingsForStorage/goalConfigForStorage helpers used by the scenario path (pkg/api/scenario.go:320-322); currently safe only because decodeStoredGeneratorAssignment/decodeStoredRuntimeSettings carry typed-nil defenses (pkg/api/stored_decode.go:203, :97) — a new decoder without that defense reintroduces the known {Mode:"auto"} typed-nil bug · dashboard/src/components/MonitoringPage.tsx:687 polls ~13 endpoints including /scenarios/schedules/health every 5 seconds; the cadence amplifies the backend full-table scan reported in this area's schedule-health finding and belongs to the frontend reviewer · pkg/storage/sqlite_schedules.go:972 has no bounded/aggregating alternative (no COUNT-by-status query) and pkg/storage has no retention pruning for scenario_schedule_occurrences; fixing the health-endpoint finding needs a storage-side status-count query or retention job

**AREA-08** — raw 8, confirmed 8, refuted 0

api-platform-core is in genuinely strong shape — this is some of the most deliberately hardened code in the repo. The websocket Hub is bounded end-to-end (client slots, send-buffer drops, fanout WG + slots, periodic re-authorization), stored_decode has explicit typed-nil guards closing the historical {Mode:"auto"} class, the settings PUT path correctly layers omitted-section merge, write-only secret preservation, tri-state thresholds, and revision-fenced CAS, server lifecycle (Start/Shutdown/launchBackground with panic recovery and no-resurrection invariants) is exemplary, and the imported-dashboard fan-out uses CAS-reserved point/byte budgets with shared semaphores. The declarative route catalog plus test-enforced fail-closed default means no registered-but-unpoliced route drift was found. The defects that remain are edge/operational rather than headline: project/test deletion misses the newest child table (powerbi_publishes), the controller-wide project-mutation gate can stall every write during a slow deletion, the idempotency layer is at-most-once rather than idempotent (failed requests burn the key), the redis rate limiter has the classic INCR/EXPIRE atomicity gap, the default in-memory cache never sweeps expired entries, and the origin policy ignores X-Forwarded-Proto so same-origin detection fails behind TLS-terminating proxies.

_Boundary leads:_ pkg/storage/sqlite_projects.go:1289-1364 (deleteProjectGraphTx) and pkg/storage/sqlite_tests.go:1323-1394 (deleteTestGraphTx) are where the powerbi_publishes cascade entries are missing — the fix for the orphaned-rows finding lands in storage, not pkg/api · pkg/api/auth_resolution.go:479 and 632 (requiredServiceAccountScopes / requiredLibraryImportServiceAccountScope) call decodeRequestBody, which io.ReadAll-buffers the ENTIRE request body (up to the 128-272 MiB import limits) into memory purely to resolve a scope, then the handler buffers/parses it again — 2x memory amplification for service-account library imports and project-scoped JSON imports; the shared body-buffering design belongs to the import areas · pkg/api/audit.go:61-64 persistAuditEvent issues a GetProject DB read on every audit event to backfill domain_id — every audited mutation platform-wide pays an extra store round-trip; worth a small cache or a domain_id pass-through from handlers that already loaded the project

**AREA-09** — raw 5, confirmed 5, refuted 0

This area is in unusually strong shape. The CI run lifecycle (ci_runs/ci_checks/ci_evidence/ci_recovery/ci_script_snapshot) is defensively engineered end to end: idempotency-keyed materialization with metadata equality checks, durable Check intents/outbox with CAS creation claims and heartbeat leases, terminal evidence gated on re-verified archive integrity, and leader-fenced recovery that never re-triggers started runs. The library federation stack (claims journal, two-phase import with compensation, immutable result archives, CAS-persisted links) is similarly rigorous, and PowerBI publish has per-test locking, drift detection, and a commit-marker runs row. External HTTP clients consistently carry timeouts, host allowlists, and bounded reads. **CC1-A** — raw 3, confirmed 3, refuted 0

Goroutine lifecycle is one of the strongest dimensions of this codebase, and that is not a hedge — it is the honest read after tracing ~90 of the 152 `go func` sites and every `go <method>()` site to their join/cancel points. The generator engine is exemplary: every VUser goroutine is WaitGroup-accounted through a single `finishReservedVUser` exit funnel (pkg/engine/group.go:1327), carries a last-resort `recoverVUserGoroutine` backstop (pkg/engine/panic_recovery.go:35), and derives an explicit four-context cancel closure (vuCtx/shedCtx/boundaryCtx + `context.AfterFunc` link that is *stopped* on exit, pkg/engine/group.go:1226-1233) so a shared-goal soft stop cannot strand a VUser; the open-workload arrival path is bounded by an in-flight limiter that sheds rather than growing goroutines (pkg/engine/group.go:566-575). The controller has a purpose-built `launchBackground` wrapper (pkg/api/server.go:1946) that accounts the goroutine in a WaitGroup, refuses admission after `beginBackgroundShutdown`, and recovers panics; shutdown then cancels each named background context and waits on explicit done channels. Worker pools are consistently fixed-size with `close(jobs)`+`wg.Wait()` and result channels buffered to the job count, so an early return never blocks a worker (pkg/api/latency.go:96-117, pkg/api/distributed_epoch.go:274-310, pkg/protocol/http/resources.go:357-400 — the last even documents why it drains rather than abandons the queue). Every `time.NewTicker` I checked has a paired `Stop`, and long-lived loops uniformly select on a quit channel or ctx. Where the discipline breaks it is not in the goroutine bodies but in the *ownership contract at the call site*: two constructors that start a goroutine hand back an object whose stopper is only reachable through one specific success/compensation path, and both have a reachable error path that returns without it. That is the whole of what I found.

**CC1-B** — raw 3, confirmed 3, refuted 0

For my specific lens - lock discipline, lock-across-I/O, and deadlock potential - this codebase is genuinely disciplined, and I want to be concrete about why rather than just assert it. Across ~970 non-test Go files and ~1,600 lock-acquisition sites I found ZERO lock-ordering inversions (28 distinct nested lock pairs, every one acquired in a consistent order in every path), ZERO RWMutex read-to-write upgrade attempts, ZERO true recursive/self-deadlock sites (all 18 machine-flagged candidates were closures, goroutine launches, or time.AfterFunc callbacks), ZERO defer-Unlock-in-a-loop-body bugs (the single candidate was a defer inside a per-iteration closure, which is correct), and ZERO unbuffered-channel sends under a held lock (all three send-under-lock sites write into freshly created cap-1 buffered channels). Several patterns are actively good practice rather than merely absent-of-bugs: the engine metrics hot path is deliberately lock-free (atomics plus sync.Map with the comment "lock-free hot-path attribution") so the 10k-goroutine target does not funnel through a mutex; pkg/protocol/http scopes its trace and per-host mutexes to a single request rather than making them package-level; shutdown paths use context-aware TryLock helpers and sync.Cond with Broadcast (not Signal) so no waiter is lost; pkg/api consistently separates a "reload serializer" mutex (contentReloadMu, testReloadMu, haScenarioRefreshMu) from the state lock tr.mu and releases tr.mu across every durable read; and pkg/distributed/generatorrpc keeps its long reconcile off the lease-renewal goroutine via an explicitly ordered callback worker. The two defects I did find are both about the *shape* of a lock rather than a missing one: one HA read-refresh path was left out of a coalescing-window fix that its three siblings all received, and one context-aware lock helper uses RWMutex.TryLock polling, which - unlike Lock() - never registers writer intent and therefore provides no bounded-acquisition guarantee.

For a 460k-LOC codebase this is the most disciplined bounded-memory work I have reviewed at the leaf level. Nearly every hot-path accumulator I traced has an explicit, named cap enforced at the single append/insert site: pkg/engine/metrics_bounds.go gives every metric dimension a 512-entry ceiling with an explicit `__other__` overflow label plus a 64 MiB snapshot-byte budget and a 3600-point snapshot ring; pkg/protocol/messaging/session.go bounds dedup by stream count (128), per-stream window (4096) AND aggregate entries with LRU eviction and a hashed stream-key so a provider-controlled destination name cannot blow the key space; pkg/protocol/http/cookie_jar.go bounds cookies per-VUser (256/64 KiB) and again process-wide (256 MiB); pkg/protocol/http/oauth.go, pkg/protocol/grpc/grpc.go, pkg/engine/secrets.go, pkg/api/archive_report_cache.go and pkg/api/group_metrics_filter.go are all entry-count + byte-budget LRUs; pkg/internal/boundedcache is a shared FIFO with key-byte accounting. The prior errorPatterns and open-workload in-flight caps are still present and still enforced (pkg/api/metrics.go:472, runner.go:1058-ish constants). Comments in ManagedTest explicitly reason about why a given map is bounded, which is unusually good. Where the discipline breaks down is one level up: the CONTROLLER's mirror of durable state. tr.tests, tr.scripts and tr.scenarios are whole-table in-memory mirrors with per-item caps but no aggregate cap and no eviction of terminal/cold items, and several hot read paths re-materialize or deep-clone the entire mirror per request/tick. The default in-process cache backend also has no expiry sweep. None of these is a leaf-level oversight; they are all 'the mirror is assumed small' assumptions that stop holding as install age and library size grow.

This backend is genuinely disciplined in the data-race dimension — more so than any other quality axis I would expect at 466k LOC. Concretely: `go vet` (full analyzer suite, including copylocks, loopclosure, atomic and waitgroup) is clean across every package in pkg/, cmd/ and desktop/; there is not a single mutation performed while only a read lock is held anywhere in the tree; there is no `sync.WaitGroup.Add` inside a goroutine literal; and every parallel fan-out I found (prometheus_graphs.go, handlers_dashboards.go, imported_dashboard_snapshots.go, distributed_inventory.go) uses the safe pre-sized-slice/distinct-index pattern rather than a shared map. The structural choices are deliberate rather than accidental: counters that are read by status endpoints are `atomic.Int64`/`atomic.Bool` (Hub.droppedClientMsgs, javasidecar Server.draining) precisely so the snapshot helpers do not need the lock; lock preconditions are encoded in method names (`*Locked`, `consumedRecordsSnapshotAssignmentLocked`, `markTestInitializingLockedWithExpectedTerm`) and I verified the convention actually holds at the call sites I sampled; the `*ManagedTest` god-object, which has no lock of its own and is guarded externally by `tr.mu`, is never handed to an HTTP handler live — every CI/read path goes through `cloneManagedTestFieldsLocked` (whose comment explicitly states why no mutable child may alias live state). Even the hard cases are right: `MultiGroupEngine.ScaleVUsers` drops `mge.mu` for a cold-start capability probe and then re-validates with a `group.VUsers != currentVUsers` CAS on re-acquire; `executionLeadership.tick` fences a delayed lease response against a stale `generation`; `ExecutionGoalLimiter` reserves/commits/releases global iteration slots atomically so a 10k-VUser run cannot overshoot its iteration goal; the WebSocket Hub's `register`/`unregister` sends both select on `h.done` so shutdown cannot wedge a client pump. My automated triage produced 292 candidate unlocked-access sites and 15 candidate inconsistently-guarded fields; every single one I traced was a false positive of my line-based lock tracker (unlock-inside-an-if, `defer` unlock, `TryLock`, or `lockRWMutexWithContext`), not a defect. I found exactly one field in the entire scope that is genuinely unsynchronised, and it has no reachable trigger today — reported below as an opportunity, not a defect. Zero defects is my honest answer for this lens.

On the Go side the largest `time.Sleep` consumer, `pkg/api/execution_backend_test.go` (34 sleeps), does not use sleep as a synchronisation barrier at all — every one sits inside a deadline-bounded poll loop that `t.Fatalf`s on timeout (e.g. lines 2313-2325, 86-96), which is the correct pattern; I found no flaky-by-construction sleep worth reporting. The 46 `t.Skip` files are overwhelmingly honest environment gates (symlink support, POSIX shell fixtures, xattr support, JDK presence), CI installs the JDK and both Playwright engines so those gates open, and the protocol-integration matrix at `.github/workflows/protocol-integration.yml:88-113` explicitly fails the job when a required secret is missing rather than letting the run no-op green. Individual tests are often better than the code they guard: `pkg/convert/paramize/heuristics_test.go:134-200` is a real got/want table including escaped-quote atomicity and template preservation; `pkg/convert/correlate/correlate_test.go:592-645` re-compiles the emitted regex and re-matches it against the source body; `pkg/api/distributed_resilience_test.go` is 1,200 lines of careful fail-closed reasoning about generator evacuation. The structural weakness is not laziness, it is **shape**: nearly every assertion is a targeted probe of a value the author already had in hand, in a fixture the author already constructed, on one side of a seam. Where a defect lives in the *composition* of two things each tested alone (web_set_user + a populated runtime config), in an *ordering* the probes cannot see (`strings.Contains` on a form body), in a *branch no fixture reaches* (an evacuation source whose RPC is dead), or on the *far side of a mocked boundary* (34 dashboard test files `vi.mock` the entire `hooks/api` transport), the suite is structurally incapable of failing — and it will keep being green after the fix phase unless the shape changes, not the count.

Worth costing the noise of turning them on incrementally. · Contract sweep owner: the generated OpenAPI spec itself is the upstream defect for the TS-contract seam — 37 of 179 request bodies emit `Record<string, unknown>` because the Go swagger annotations do not declare a body schema. Fixing the dashboard types cannot succeed until the annotations do. `pkg/api/handlers_execution_plans.go` is the smallest reproducer. · Frontend sweep owner: `dashboard/src/components/scenarioFormModel.ts` holds a confirmed High (scenarioFormModel.ts:56, silent group deletion) and has no test file at all, while its consumers (NewTestPage, TestHub) are heavily tested through mocked hooks. It is the clearest case where the model layer, not the component layer, is the right test target. · Distributed/concurrency sweep owner: `metricsAggregateSetHasEvidence` / the no-new-evidence replay at pkg/distributed/generatorrpc/service.go:2156-2171 has zero test references by any name; the Highs list flags it. This is not a bad test suite; it is a suite optimized for the wrong unit. The genuinely strong work is easy to find: pkg/storage/sqlite_deletion_durability_test.go:11 installs a live SQLite trigger to force a mid-transaction abort and then proves the reservation release and archive-cleanup outbox rolled back atomically, and a whole family of TestConcurrent*CreateAnd*DeleteCannotLeaveOrphan tests (sqlite_application_release_integrity_test.go:121, sqlite_authoring_session_integrity_test.go:78, sqlite_datapool_parent_integrity_test.go:28/82, sqlite_capacity_bindings_atomic_test.go:238) drive real create-vs-delete interleavings against a real store; pkg/protocol/soap/soap_test.go:296/392/428 spin up httptest servers and assert fault code, category, telemetry, snapshot redaction AND a true-negative case; pkg/api/runner_test.go:4593 explicitly guards against a broadcast deadlock under the runner lock; CommandCenterPrototype.test.tsx runs 30+ genuine interaction tests against a real React tree rather than snapshots. These are tests written by people who understood the failure modes. The structural weakness is that every one of them exercises ONE feature against a MINIMAL fixture, and the confirmed defects live at feature INTERSECTIONS. I checked all 285 confirmed defects against the tree: 190 of them (67%), including 16 of the 30 Highs, sit in files that already have a co-located test file, and those files are not thinly tested - the median co-located test is 886 lines and the six worst-hit files carry 1,648-to-6,456-line test files. So coverage is not the binding constraint and adding more tests of the current shape will not help; this corroborates lens CC4-A. Three independent subsystems show the identical mechanism: the deletion test builds Project+Test+Reservation+Archive but never attaches a schedule, so the schedule FK High (sqlite_tests.go:1390) walks past a test file built specifically to verify deletion; TestConvertMapsWebSetUserToHTTPAuth passes an empty ConvertOptions{} so the destructive HTTPConfig branch that wipes the auth it asserts is unreachable; and every one of the 16 SOAP tests omits DiscardResponseBodyOnSuccess, which production always sets. The suite composes at most one feature at a time; the bugs need two.

_Boundary leads:_ CC4-A (test design): my correlation is direct corroboration - 190/285 defects and 16/30 Highs are in files that already have co-located tests with a median of 886 test lines. A contract-generation fix and a transport-test fix are the same remedy; whoever owns the seam should own both. · Completeness critic (hooks/api structurally unowned): confirmed and quantified - 16 of 19 modules, 151 endpoint templates, 5,141 LOC untested; useTestApi.ts (914 LOC, 47 endpoints, the entire run lifecycle) is the single highest-value target. · Whoever owns pkg/api/openapi_contract_infer.go: it carries 5 confirmed defects and has NO co-located test file at all, while being the generator that produces docs/swagger.yaml and openapi.ts. Any 'concurrency verified CLEAN' conclusion elsewhere should be read as 'no race was executed', not 'no race exists'.

All 15 consumers compile against the real 3.9.2 typings with no leftover v2-only props: nobody uses `alwaysShow` (every reference element uses `ifOverflow`), nobody reaches for `Customized`, `Tooltip`/`Legend` are used with props that still exist, `layout="vertical"` BarChart in ReportCharts.tsx correctly declares `XAxis type="number"` + `YAxis type="category"`, and the two `content` render-props (TestHub's `ScenarioModelTooltip`, TestExecutionCharts' `content={() => null}`) match v3's `TooltipContentProps` shape exactly. The Go dependency posture is, with one exception, unusually disciplined for a tree this size, and most of the things this lens normally catches were already handled deliberately. The toolchain is pinned end-to-end (go.mod `go 1.26.5`, `GOTOOLCHAIN: local` in every workflow, `go-version-file: go.mod` at all 11 setup-go sites, digest-pinned golang:1.26.5-alpine builder), so there is no compiler-version skew to find. cel-go 0.29.2 is bounded on all three axes an untrusted-expression evaluator needs (ParserExpressionSizeLimit, ParserRecursionLimit, and `cel.CostLimit(10_000)` which I verified at cel-go@v0.29.2/cel/options.go:769 does set `OptTrackCost` itself, so the limit is genuinely armed). The go-redis v9.21.0 rate limiter is now a single Lua script doing INCR+PTTL+PEXPIRE atomically, the LoadOrStore script correctly distinguishes Lua `false` from an empty value, and `redis.Nil` is handled via `errors.Is` at the one read path. gopsutil is used with full awareness that it is host-scoped: the collector supplements it with a hand-rolled cgroup v1/v2 reader for container CPU limit, throttling, memory working set and OOM kills, which is exactly the right call for a K8s-native tool. Postgres pool defaults are documented in README, the enterprise plan, and set concretely (25/10/30m) in every shipped Helm/K8s manifest. gocloud blob writers return `Close()`'s error on the success path and close on the failure path. parquet-go `WriteStop()` is called on every exit path in both writers. azeventhubs/v2's `StartPosition` earliest-vs-latest trap is handled and commented. franz-go's `Close()` needs no preceding `Flush` here because every produce goes through `ProduceSync`. goquery 1.12.0 is a dependency-refresh-only release per its own README changelog, so nothing to migrate. The one real failure is the Playwright pin: the Go module was moved forward to v0.6100.0 (driver 1.61.1) without moving the npm driver alias that the container actually ships, and both the Dockerfile guard and the CI assertion were written against the stale number, so the drift is now actively enforced rather than caught. Beyond that, the two findings I have are library-semantics mismatches at specific call sites rather than upgrade regressions.

Documentation-shaped, not a defect.

**GAPFE-1** — raw 8, confirmed 8, refuted 0

The megafile is genuinely well-guarded in most places -- the two request-token maps, the per-item review/replay generation tuples, and the source-secret discard bookkeeping are all coherent, and the three defect classes the critic guessed at (frozen-const identity leaks, save-index drift on remove/re-add, truncation misclassification in looksLikeJavaSource) are NOT real. But the guards are asymmetric in two specific ways that do bite: (a) a single-item fence bumps a GLOBAL operation generation, so touching one queue row aborts an in-flight durable write on a different row; (b) a scope check that correctly suppresses a stale response ALSO suppresses the cleanup of the loading flag that response was supposed to clear, permanently pinning the item. Separately, this surface is the only importer in the codebase that drops the backend's replay preflight envelope entirely.

_Boundary leads:_ ProtocolAssetImport.tsx (~:365) prefers the top-level result.preflight over the per-script metadata fallback. pkg/api/handlers_import_shared.go:53-74 confirms the envelope carries only the AGGREGATE script's preflight while each generated lane carries its own at metadata.import.preserved.replay_preflight, so a mixed Kafka/JMS AsyncAPI import renders the first lane's preflight on every tab. Belongs to whoever owns ProtocolAssetImport, not this file. · Multi-script import_draft_expires_at contract: EnterpriseArchiveImport.tsx:2675 and :2775 both drop the server's refreshed import_draft_expires_at when nextScripts.length > 1, because the server returns a per-script expiry (applySecretBindings / applyImportParameterization) with no defined aggregate semantics. Consequence at the UI layer: ScriptImportReview.tsx:389/403/417 hard-disables Save AND Edit once the ORIGINAL window lapses, so a long multi-lane Java review can self-lock even after the user refreshed individual lanes. Needs a backend decision on what the aggregate expiry should be before the frontend can be fixed. · Client/server Java sniff window divergence: EnterpriseArchiveImport.tsx:87 caps at 256*1024 JS string CHARACTERS while pkg/convert/enterprisearchive/java_source_names.go:92 caps at 256<<10 BYTES, and the server additionally strips a UTF-8 BOM at line 91 that the client only gets for free via Blob.text(). For a windows-1252 or CJK-commented source the two windows cover different amounts of the file, so the client-displayed resolved name can disagree with the name the server actually stores. Low impact but the two comments claim to mirror each other. · EnterpriseArchiveImport.tsx:1080 tests availableNames.has(expectedPath) against candidate.suggestedPath (e.g. 'com/foo/Bar.java'), but File.name from <input type=file> and from filesFromDroppedPaths is always a bare basename, so that half of the match can never fire. Whether the backend ever reports path-qualified supplemental names is a server-contract question.

**GAPFE-2** — raw 8, confirmed 8, refuted 0

CommandCenterPrototype.tsx is a mockup that was promoted to the production live-control surface, and the seams show exactly where the promotion was incomplete. The plumbing added for live mode is careful: the run-poll and auto-discovery effects both have visibility gating, in-flight guards, generation refs and complete cleanups; the group-settings dialog is explicitly unbound on run switch (:980); the canonical-target sync at :1148-1165 correctly preserves an operator's in-progress edit against every poll tick (the D021 defect class does NOT apply here); usePrometheusGraphs/useImportedDashboardGraphs are deliberately starved in non-live modes so the mock never hits the network. What was not revisited is the prototype's numeric furniture. The VUser target control still clamps at the mock's 2,400 ceiling while the product's real ceiling is 1,000,000 and the sibling surface (useExecutionLiveControls:101) refuses out-of-range values instead of silently rewriting them - that one sends a wrong scale command to a live run. A hard-coded MOCK_LIVE_METRICS.error_pct still backstops the headline Error Rate pill, so a run that has not produced its first metrics sample displays a plausible 1.02% next to a hero card reading 0.00%. The 'loading' test object is a spread of MOCK_TEST, so a 404 on the routed run leaves a shelf advertising a 1h duration, 37m 18s remaining and live Stop/Abort buttons that only mutate local state. Two more surfaces fabricate numbers that look measured: the Scenario Run table synthesizes Target TPS as tps x 1.12 (the mock's own constant) for every vuser-driven group and reports a permanent 10.71% throughput gap, and the Load Model panel invents the planned-load curve and grades the run against it. Separately, the error drill-down keys its selection on the array index of a list the backend re-sorts by count, so the selection jumps away mid-triage. The file is not rotten - the live wiring is real and mostly sound - but every value it prints needs to be re-derived from the run instead of from the demo fixture.

_Boundary leads:_ pkg/api/goal_controller.go:423 - applyRuntimeGoalTargetsToLiveMetrics returns early unless ScenarioMode == 'goal_oriented', so GroupLiveMetrics.target_tps (pkg/api/runner.go:967, omitempty) is never populated for vuser-driven runs even when the run has stage-driven throughput expectations. The UI defect I report (#5) is a frontend fabrication and must be fixed in the frontend, but a backend-published per-group target_tps (or an explicit null) would let every consumer stop guessing. · pkg/api/handlers.go:99,115,124 - handleListTests only sets prioritizeActive when the caller passes an explicit limit, so a caller that omits limit gets the 200 newest tests by created_at with no active-first ordering. Any UI that discovers running work through this endpoint is at the mercy of run-creation volume. Worth deciding backend-side whether active runs should always sort first regardless of limitExplicit; the frontend half of this is my finding #4. · pkg/api/runner.go:917 - LiveErrorPattern.EvidenceCount is `json:"evidence_count,omitempty"`, so a pattern with zero captured evidence is indistinguishable from a pattern that never reported the field. dashboard/src/components/CommandCenterPrototype.tsx:2586 and :2636 both fall back to an unrelated length because of it. Dropping omitempty on this counter would remove a whole class of UI guesswork. · pkg/api/live_error_evidence.go:250-255 - liveErrorPatternsList re-sorts patterns by Count desc on every tick with no stable identifier in the payload. My finding #3 is fixable client-side by keying on signature, but a server-assigned stable pattern id would be the durable fix and would also help the archive/report renderers.

**GAPFE-3** — raw 8, confirmed 8, refuted 0

MonitoringPage.tsx (2,599 lines) is a genuine three-area orphan and it does carry real defects, but not the ones the file's size suggests. The refresh machinery is better engineered than expected: runCoalescedRefresh (:367-388) genuinely prevents overlapping in-flight polls and poll backlogs, every refresh callback dep is reference-stable (api comes from a memoized context provider, calendarRange from a useMemo) so the 5s interval at :687 is NOT torn down on every render and there is no stale-closure bug, and a generation+project-scope guard (:526-528, :638) discards results from a superseded project. The threshold-alert acknowledgement path is also sound end-to-end: acknowledged survives re-upsert while the entry stays active (thresholdAlerts.ts:91-97) and stale per-transaction entries are resolved one metrics cycle later (App.tsx:508-521). The real damage is concentrated in the run-calendar block: it buckets events into day cells by the viewer's local midnight while labelling them in the event's own declared timezone (the inert-timezone class), the Day view renders the whole fetched range instead of the anchored day, the model rebuild is O(days x events) with per-comparison Date parsing on a 5-second cadence against a 2,000-event server cap, and any calendar navigation re-issues a 13-endpoint refreshAll whose results are applied only after all 13 settle. Two cross-cutting reliability gaps round it out: the initial full load is silently skipped forever if the page mounts while the tab is hidden (and the only recovery path refreshes just the active category, leaving never-fetched fleet state rendered as 'clear'), and the day-cell role=button wrapper swallows keyboard activation of the run chips nested inside it.

_Boundary leads:_ pkg/api/run_calendar.go:17 runCalendarMaxEvents=2000 with no server-side per-day aggregation: the client is handed up to 2,000 fully-hydrated events (each carrying Workload.Groups, User, and Topology incl. generator_inventory) every 5 seconds while the Schedules tab is open. A day-bucketed or summary projection (counts per day + events for the focused day) would remove the client-side O(days x events) rebuild entirely. Backend-owned. · pkg/api/run_calendar.go:815 and :958 set RunCalendarEvent.Timezone only for projected cron and execution-plan events; materialized occurrences and ad-hoc runs carry an empty timezone. The frontend therefore mixes two rendering rules inside one grid (event-zone for projections, browser-local for everything else). A backend decision on whether Timezone should also be stamped on materialized occurrences would let the UI pick one consistent rule. · pkg/api/system_services.go never emits a service with kind 'frontend', so the dashboard row is always synthesized client-side from window.location.origin. If the backend emitted the served-dashboard origin (it knows it when it serves the SPA), the client-side merge heuristic in MonitoringPage.tsx:2547-2567 could be deleted rather than fixed.

**GAPFE-4** — raw 8, confirmed 8, refuted 0

The API-client layer itself is in better shape than the gap report implies: apiClient.ts, useTestApi.ts and useScriptApi.ts are almost entirely thin, dependency-free useCallback wrappers with correct useMemo dep arrays, so hook identity does not churn and ProjectProvider/ApplicationProvider already carry explicit scope+generation guards (ApplicationProvider.tsx:26-34, 60-67, 91-96). The real defect cluster is one level up, at the read seam: the server-side pagination contract (/tests default limit 200 + `total`, /object-repositories, /correlation-rulesets, /capacity/timeslots default 100 with no `total` at all) is exposed by the hooks but consumed as if complete by nearly every caller. useSharedTestList surfaces count/total/limit/offset faithfully, yet exactly one of its three consumers (ResultsPage.tsx:373) checks for truncation; DashboardPage derives headline release KPI tiles from a client-side filter over a server-truncated window. A second, smaller cluster is that apiClient's `request()` accepts an AbortSignal but every one of the ~200 domain-hook wrappers drops the options argument, forcing each consumer to hand-roll a generation guard -- which most do, and at least one (TimeslotsPanel) does not.

_Boundary leads:_ pkg/api/handlers.go:99 couples active-run hoisting to the *presence* of an explicit limit (`prioritizeActive: limitExplicit`). Any caller that omits `limit` gets pure created-at-desc ordering plus the 200 cap, which is the opposite of what an omitted-limit caller usually wants. Backend-side fix: always prioritize active, or document the coupling in the route catalog/swagger. · pkg/api/handlers_object_repository.go:96, pkg/api/handlers_correlation_rulesets.go:257-266 and pkg/api/handlers_timeslots.go:190-195 return only {count, limit, offset} and no `total`, so no frontend can detect truncation on these three list endpoints even if it wanted to. /tests already returns `total` (handlers.go:118); these should match it. · pkg/api/handlers_correlation_rulesets.go:27 hard-caps maxCorrelationRulesetListLimit at 100, so a client cannot widen the page at all; paging is only possible via offset, which no dashboard surface implements. · pkg/api/handlers.go:841-861 (/scripts) and the /scenarios list are entirely unbounded -- the opposite scale hazard from /tests. A project with thousands of scripts returns the full masked corpus in one response to ScriptsPage, TestHub, BrunoImport, ProtocolAssetImport (x2), TestExecutionScenarioEditor and the per-project repository-catalog fan-out. · pkg/api/tests.go:558-566: when application_id/release_id/scenario_id is supplied, project_id is ignored for filtering (contextFiltered short-circuits the project branch). Harmless today because every caller that sends application_id also owns the project, but it is an undocumented precedence rule the frontend silently relies on.

**GAPFE-5** — raw 8, confirmed 8, refuted 0

ScriptEditorParameterFeatures.tsx is the parameter-authoring surface for the script editor: eight exported dialogs/panels plus the shared PARAMETER_CHOICE_DEFINITIONS enum table. The enum table itself is in good shape for the mutable fields (update/selection/on_exhaustion exactly match pkg/dsl/validate.go:1130-1138) and parameter *type* is deliberately read-only in every panel, which structurally avoids the D007 rewrite class for types. The defects concentrate elsewhere: (a) one panel, SelectedParameterDetails, edits parameters through a generic key/value reflection loop whose type table is wrong, so it writes strings into array/number DSL fields; (b) the ParameterDataDialog auto-select effects fight the user when a parameter's data_source changes, moving edits onto a different parameter; (c) several round-trips (inline list values, time format presets, parameter->data-source strategy sync) are lossy. Nothing here is security-relevant. Two of the findings are ones an operator hits on ordinary first-use paths, not exotic sequences.

_Boundary leads:_ dashboard/src/components/ScriptEditor.tsx:4233 applyAutoParameterization replaces candidate literals with String.split(value).join(token) per field. If one selected candidate's value is a substring of another's (e.g. an account id '10045' and the URL segment '/orders/10045/items'), applying the shorter candidate first rewrites the longer candidate's literal, so the longer candidate silently applies to nothing and its {{data.auto_params.*}} column is created with a seed row but no reference. Ordering is the array order of parameterCandidates, not longest-first. Primary cause is in ScriptEditor.tsx, outside this probe's file. · dashboard/src/components/ScriptEditorParameterDataSources.tsx:347 the source-level 'Iteration strategy' select offers only sequential/random/unique, but pkg/engine/data.go:261 accepts 'pop' as a data-source strategy with distinct stop-after-exhaustion semantics. An imported source with strategy 'pop' renders with a value matching no option and is rewritten on the first change. This is the D005 file, likely in that finding's scope. · pkg/dsl/validate.go:1126 and pkg/dsl/parameters.go:34 make 'vuser_id' a first-class canonical parameter type (LR 'VuserID'/'Vuser Num' normalize to it), but no frontend surface can create one. Whether the importer actually emits vuser_id for real LR scripts is a backend question worth confirming before sizing the frontend gap.
